title: Define a Safe Learning Task
why: A measurable low-stakes task makes it possible to judge whether ML adds value.
activity: Choose a low-stakes prediction problem using open or synthetic data. Define the target, error costs, intended use, and prohibited uses.
evidence: A task specification and initial risk assessment.
reflection: What kind of error would make this model inappropriate for its intended use?

title: Understand the Numerical Foundations
why: Understanding the numerical steps helps you diagnose unexpected model behavior.
activity: Implement a small numerical exercise related to your task, such as linear prediction and a loss calculation. Check outputs by hand on a tiny example.
evidence: An explained numerical exercise with manually verified outputs.
reflection: Which calculation did you check manually, and what did it reveal?

title: Establish a Simple Baseline
why: A simple baseline sets a minimum standard for model usefulness.
activity: Implement a majority, mean, or rule-based baseline. Define evaluation metrics before training and explain why a complex model may be unnecessary.
evidence: Baseline code, metric definitions, and reproducible baseline results.
reflection: Why is your chosen baseline a meaningful comparison?

title: Prepare Data Without Leakage
why: Leakage can make evaluation appear strong without useful generalization.
activity: Document provenance and permission. Split data appropriately for time, groups, or samples; fit preprocessing on training data only and check for leakage.
evidence: A data preparation pipeline, split protocol, and leakage checks.
reflection: Which preprocessing or split decision could accidentally expose test information?

title: Run Controlled Experiments
why: Controlled experiments let you attribute changes to a specific decision.
activity: Train a simple model and a small set of controlled variants. Record seeds, configuration, training data version, and validation results. Keep test data held out.
evidence: A training script and experiment log with comparable runs.
reflection: Which comparison isolated an effect, rather than changing several things at once?

title: Evaluate Failures and Trade-offs
why: Average performance can conceal important failures and coverage gaps.
activity: Evaluate the selected model once on held-out data. Compare with the baseline, examine failures, and discuss subgroup coverage and uncertainty.
evidence: An evaluation report with baseline comparison and error examples.
reflection: Which error pattern matters most for the intended use?

title: Document Responsible Use
why: Documented limitations help people avoid uses the model was never tested for.
activity: Write a model card covering intended use, limitations, privacy, fairness, and misuse. Propose a mitigation and test at least one relevant risk.
evidence: A model card, risk test, and mitigation evidence.
reflection: Which risk did you test, and what evidence supports your mitigation?

title: Package a Local Inference Demo
why: A model needs predictable input, output, and failure behavior to be usable.
activity: Build a local inference interface with input validation, a clear contract, and failure handling. Measure latency on your device; no paid cloud deployment is required.
evidence: A runnable local demo, input/output contract, and latency measurements.
reflection: How does your interface behave on an invalid or unfamiliar input?

title: Plan Monitoring and Human Review
why: Changing inputs can invalidate yesterday’s evaluation.
activity: Define checks for input shifts, failing predictions, and misuse. Specify when to fall back, stop the model, or request human review; test one failure scenario.
evidence: A monitoring/fallback plan and a demonstrated failure scenario.
reflection: What observable signal should trigger fallback or human review?

title: Create an ML Case Study
why: An ML portfolio needs reproducible evidence and honest limits, not a single impressive score.
activity: Connect task framing, data, baseline, experiments, evaluation, responsible use, and deployment limits. Distinguish measured performance from claims outside the dataset.
evidence: A reproducible ML case study, model card, and reviewable demo.
reflection: Which performance claim would fail outside your evaluation setting?
